title: human in the loop — under agents

tracks.title: A run that waits for a person
tracks.text: Lesson 05 point 6 — human in the loop. A sub-lesson, under agents. The agents lesson ended on a promise — agents, not autopilot… trust earned in increments. This is the mechanics of that promise. A run that waits for a person. [curious] The problem is that autonomy is almost always binary. Either you babysit every step — which is a chat window with extra ceremony — or the agent commits blind and you review the wreckage after. What's missing is the middle. A checkpoint inside a live run, where the agent keeps its momentum… but one decision blocks on a human. No notification service. No queue. No human pretending to be an A-P-I. Just three small primitives… and a command that waits.

tracks.title: The definition
tracks.text: The definition. A human-in-the-loop checkpoint is three things. First… a canvas the agent opens for a human to judge. Second… a commit the human makes, carrying the approved state plus a note. Third… a mailbox — the run's own session — that the agent polls until the verdict arrives. And here's the reframe that makes it work. The human's verdict is data. Not remote control. They never reach in and drive the agent's mouse. They approve a state — a set of values — and they leave a note. The runtime hands that back to the agent as a small piece of J-SON. [curious] Judgment is the human's job. The labor of turning judgment into source edits stays with the agent. The worked example, all the way through, is C-T-K — the canvas toolkit. Its whole tagline is… a human-in-the-loop canvas. And one honest flag up front — everything here is experimental. We'll come back to exactly how young at the end.

tracks.title: A run with an address
tracks.text: First primitive — a run with an address. Nothing else works without it. Every run can be named… and the agent inside it knows its own name. Picture the flow. A request comes in — POST slash A-P-I slash run — and the runtime answers two-oh-two immediately, with an id… run forty-one seventeen, status running. Behind that id sits exactly one supervised process — the session — keyed by the run id in a registry. And here's the deliberate move. When the session starts the agent, it injects the run's own id into the agent's environment, as W-B underscore RUN. The comment in the source says it plainly — W-B RUN lets the agent address its own run for C-T-K reviews. So the picture is three boxes top to bottom. The request mints the session. The session spawns the agent, with W-B RUN set to run forty-one seventeen. And a dotted arrow loops back up — the agent can now hand out a U-R-L that names the very session that owns it. That id is the thread… tying a human's verdict to your run. Not another session. [excited] Yours.

tracks.title: The review canvas
tracks.text: Next — the review canvas. This is what the human actually looks at. C-T-K is a toolkit of kind render — a fixed shell, never designed per story. A top bar… a left control panel… a stage. It is deliberately not for shipping apps, and not for C-L-I automation. It inserts one checkpoint into the agent loop, for one isolated artifact. Now a story is one Org file doing double duty. A Controls table declares the panel… and a tangle source block carries the component itself. The shell parses the table to build the controls, and imports the tangled source to render the stage. Let me read you the real button story. The controls table has four rows. First… label, a text input, defaulting to Download. Second… variant, a select, defaulting to primary, choosing between primary, ghost, and danger. Third… accent, a color, defaulting to a blue hex. Fourth… size, a range slider, default fourteen, from eleven to twenty. Then a disabled state, with an override, carrying its own per-state control — opacity, a slider from zero to one. And below all that… a begin-source J-S block, tangling to component dot js, exporting render. [excited] Here's the punchline. The table is the review UI. Nobody designed a form. The tangle block is the component under review. There are five control types in all — text, color, range, toggle, and select — and the range and select types carry a little grammar for their bounds and their options. And the reference file, c-t-k dot html, is self-contained — you can open it bare, with no runtime at all. That self-sufficiency is exactly what lets the commit step degrade gracefully.

tracks.title: One event, two transports
tracks.text: One event… two transports. When the human is happy, they hit Commit, write an optional note — what's right, what to change — and confirm. What leaves the canvas is a single c-t-k dot commit event. Let me read it to you. Type… c-t-k dot commit. Story… button. Feedback… ghost variant border is too faint, bump to line-strong. Then the snapshot — the approved state — holding the props, label Download, variant ghost, accent blue, size fourteen… and the states, each with its effective props. And finally a timestamp in milliseconds. Two fields carry the meaning. The snapshot is the full approved page state. The feedback is the human's note — which may be empty. And C-T-K sends this over two transports at once, so it works embedded or standalone. One — a host post-message to the parent frame, when it lives inside another frame. Two — a connector webhook, when it's loaded standalone with connect equals a U-R-L. It posts the J-SON, and a two-hundred-class reply means delivered. And if there's neither a host nor a connector? [chuckles] The payload is captured to the console, the button reads shared locally, and the bench never blocks. The thing that routes a verdict to the right run is the query string — run equals W-B RUN, on the connect U-R-L. So the sequence reads like this. The human tunes the controls and commits. The canvas posts the event to the commit route, with run forty-one seventeen in the query. The runtime drops it into that session's mailbox — put review — and answers two-oh-two. Now hear the route contract as a pair. Posting a commit returns two-oh-two when delivered, four hundred if the run id is missing, four-oh-four if there's no such run. And getting a review returns two hundred with the event, two-oh-four when nothing's pending yet, four-oh-four for no such run. [curious] Notice the asymmetry — it explains the whole design. The post is an append — it adds a verdict. The get is a destructive pop — it takes the oldest pending verdict and removes it. One half feeds a mailbox. The other half drains it. [curious]

tracks.title: The run's mailbox
tracks.text: Now the depth rung — the run's mailbox. This is where the verdict stops being ephemeral. The session process is the mailbox. The web side calls put review. The agent side calls take review. A first-in first-out queue sits between them. But put review doesn't just enqueue — a single review fans out to four places, each with a different job. First… a live push to web-socket subscribers, so anyone watching the stream sees it the instant it lands. Second… the reviews queue itself, popped oldest-first — that's the poller, exactly-once delivery to the agent. Third… an append-only review log on the run's status, surfaced both while the run is live and after it finishes — the run's permanent record. And fourth… a per-run J-SON-L file on disk, a durable trace that outlives the run process — best-effort. The verdict of those four destinations, in one breath — a single approval is pushed live, queued for the agent, kept on the record, and written to disk. It is never lost to the ether. Take review pops the oldest pending review and returns nothing when empty — a destructive, exactly-once read, aimed at the poller. And that disk write is wrapped so a failure quietly succeeds — it can never crash the session. [whispers] It's a record… not a recovery mechanism. Hold that distinction — the honest section comes back to it.

tracks.title: The blocking command
tracks.text: Next — the blocking command. This is how the agent waits. And here's the constraint that shapes everything. An agent in this ecosystem has exactly one tool. Bash. No callback to register. No webhook for the agent to host. No long-poll framework. So… wait for a human… has to collapse into a single blocking command. The line is — w-b c-t-k await, dollar W-B RUN. It blocks up to six hundred seconds, until the human clicks Commit. Under the hood it polls the review route every two seconds. A two-oh-four means keep waiting. A two hundred with a body means pretty-print the review and succeed. And when the deadline passes — default six hundred seconds — it exits non-zero, timed out waiting for a review. Picture the sequence. Await asks the runtime — anything? Two-oh-four, nothing yet. Sleep two seconds. Asks again — two-oh-four, still nothing. Sleep two seconds… up to six hundred. Asks again — and this time, two hundred, carrying the commit event. Print it, exit clean. That diagram is the whole verb. Ask… get two-oh-four… sleep two… until a two hundred carries the verdict, or six hundred seconds turns it into a failure. And because the agent only has bash, the same contract is just a raw loop — a while loop that curls the review route, breaks the moment the body is non-empty, and sleeps two seconds otherwise. An empty body is a two-oh-four is not yet. A non-empty body is the event. [chuckles] Wait for a human… really is just a poll loop wearing a command's clothes.

tracks.title: The whole loop, once
tracks.text: Now the signature — the whole loop, once. This is the diagram the page is remembered by. Four players — agent, canvas, runtime, and human. Walk it as a story. The agent edits the component, then writes the C-T-K story. It prints a connect U-R-L, with run forty-one seventeen baked in, and hands it to the human. Then it calls await, and blocks. The human opens the canvas, tunes the props and the per-state values, and hits Commit with a note. That posts to the commit route. Await unblocks, and hands the agent the event — a two hundred. The agent reads the snapshot and the feedback… translates them into real source edits… and commits, using the feedback as the commit message. Let me read you the actual recipe. Echo the review U-R-L. Set review equals w-b c-t-k await — it blocks. Pipe the review through j-q to pull dot feedback — ghost variant border is too faint, bump to line-strong. Pipe it again for dot snapshot — the approved props and per-state values. Translate the approved state into source edits. Then git add, git commit, with the feedback as the message. The cardinal rule, in C-T-K's own words — C-T-K never edits your files. It returns the human-approved state plus a note. You translate that into source edits and the commit. The snapshot is the approved state — props and per-state values — not the source. And the pitfall worth tattooing on your wrist. Drop run equals W-B RUN from the connect U-R-L… and the commit has nowhere to route. Await waits the full six hundred seconds and exits one… for nothing. The run id is load-bearing, because it's the only thing tying a verdict to this run.

tracks.title: When the agent moves the sliders
tracks.text: A second depth rung — when the agent moves the sliders. A human moves the controls. But so can the agent. And there's a deliberate choice hiding here — there is no separate automation A-P-I. The controls a human moves, and the ones a driver sets, are the same props. The agent doesn't propose changes through a back door. It sets the same dials the human will then judge, through a small in-page surface called window dot C-T-K. What's on that surface? First… stories, current, and load — which stories exist, which is showing, and switch to one. Second… spec, controls, and states — read the panel. Third… props, state-props, and get — read the current values. Fourth… set, and set-state-prop — write a value, coerced by the control's declared type. And fifth… snapshot — capture the full effective state for the record. Across frames, the same surface speaks post-message — an action of load, set, or snapshot going in, a snapshot reply coming back. And the runtime loop is five steps. Serve the canvas. Read the spec. Propose, by setting values. Observe — the human sees the stage, a snapshot keeps the record. Then approve, or iterate. [excited] Because proposing and judging touch the identical props, the agent can stage a starting point, and the human adjusts from there. No translation layer between what the driver set… and what the human saw.

tracks.title: Where the loop is thin
tracks.text: Now the honest part — where the loop is thin. Full honesty. This is the most experimental thing on these pages. Marked status experimental, across the manifest and every skill, with the note — mark stable once a real run commits an approved change. The thin spots are real, and worth naming. First… the queue lives in session memory. If the session process dies while you're mid-review, there's no true resume — the queue went with it. Second… the disk file is a record, not a recovery. That per-run J-SON-L is a best-effort trace — it quietly succeeds even on failure. It tells you what happened. It doesn't rebuild a lost run. Third… nobody notifies the human. The agent prints a U-R-L. A person has to actually open it. There is no notification channel — that's a gap, stated plainly. Fourth… the verdict carries no reviewer identity. Auth is the bearer token on the route, not a signature on the verdict. The event records what was approved… not provably who approved it. And fifth — the most honest one. The env seam is plumbed, but unverified end to end. The session injects W-B RUN into the agent's run options, and the recipe reads it. But whether it actually expands inside the agent's in-WASM shell today… is the open question. The skill's own gap note says the injection is wired, and a live round-trip — real run, human commit, agent commit — is the remaining verification. We'd rather flag that, than imply it's proven. None of this contradicts the design. It scopes it. The three primitives are right, and small. The maturity is young. Believe the shape… not a ships-itself story.

tracks.title: Questions people actually ask
tracks.text: Quick fire. [curious] What if the human never clicks? Await blocks up to six hundred seconds, then exits non-zero. The agent decides — re-prompt with a fresh U-R-L, or abort. The timeout is a deadline, not a hang. Can the human edit the code in the canvas? No — and that's the boundary that keeps responsibility clean. The human approves a state, and leaves a note. The agent translates that into source edits and commits. Human, judgment. Agent, labor. Where does the approval live afterward? On the run's record — an append-only review log surfaced in the run's status, running and finished, plus a per-run file on disk. Tomorrow you can read the whole episode back. Can one run have multiple checkpoints? Yes. The mailbox is a queue — commits stack up, and the agent pops them oldest-first, exactly once each. And — is this the same as approving each tool call? No. Coarser, and better. A per-tool dialog interrupts constantly and shows you a verb, not an outcome. [chuckles] A checkpoint shows you a rendered artifact, at a meaningful moment, and asks one question. Is this right? You judge the result… not the mechanism.

tracks.title: Back up to agents
tracks.text: So that's human in the loop. Three small primitives — a run with an address, a verdict that's data, and a session that's a mailbox. And because the agent has exactly one tool, wait for a human collapses into one blocking command. [curious] If any of it felt unfamiliar, the way back up is short. This is the mechanics behind one line in the parent lesson — agents, not autopilot. So go back to agents, lesson five, for the worker this checkpoint pauses. The human brings the judgment. The agent brings the labor. And the runtime… is just the membrane between them.
